   That evening, Annie Andrews, the Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina, said in a televised debate: “To set the record straight, I don’t support Medicare for All.”

As a presidential candidate in 2020, Joe Biden said he would veto any Medicare for All bill as too costly and disruptive, while then-candidate Kamala Harris, an early supporter, soon softened her position.

   This year, Democratic socialists and others on the party’s left flank are calling for Medicare for All. But in many of the competitive states and districts now represented by Republicans, the Democrats trying to flip those seats are taking a more centrist position, akin to Biden’s. They say they would work to boost subsidies under the Affordable Care Act so that more people could buy private insurance. Some would allow more people to opt in to Medicare—a measure shy of Medicare for All as Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent, defines it. He wants a government-run, single-payer system that would overtake most private insurance.

   A recent Wall Street Journal poll that tested support for more than 30 policy ideas found that the three most popular had to do with healthcare. But Medicare for All wasn’t among them. Rather, the most popular ideas—drawing more than 80% among both parties and independents—were banning surprise medical bills, capping drug prices and requiring insurers to cover the services that doctors prescribe. Only 23% of Republicans supported Medicare for All, a caution for any candidate who needs some measure of Republican support to win in November.

Medicare for All Is the Big Policy Fight Splitting Democrats
 
Plus, Ken Paxton partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice, and federal agents searched Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home
 
 
SARAH RICE/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. I’m Aaron Zitner, a reporter and editor in our Washington Bureau, filling in for Damian Paletta this week to bring you some of the developments we’re seeing in the midterm campaign.

 

Facing a rowdy crowd Sunday in Maine, Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate, declared: “I want Medicare for All.”

 

That evening, Annie Andrews, the Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina, said in a televised debate: “To set the record straight, I don’t support Medicare for All.”

 

Medicare for All has become a defining policy fight within the Democratic Party—and a measuring stick of how far to the left the party wants to move. As a presidential candidate in 2020, Joe Biden said he would veto any Medicare for All bill as too costly and disruptive, while then-candidate Kamala Harris, an early supporter, soon softened her position.

 

This year, Democratic socialists and others on the party’s left flank are calling for Medicare for All. But in many of the competitive states and districts now represented by Republicans, the Democrats trying to flip those seats are taking a more centrist position, akin to Biden’s. They say they would work to boost subsidies under the Affordable Care Act so that more people could buy private insurance. Some would allow more people to opt in to Medicare—a measure shy of Medicare for All as Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent, defines it. He wants a government-run, single-payer system that would overtake most private insurance.

 

A recent Wall Street Journal poll that tested support for more than 30 policy ideas found that the three most popular had to do with healthcare. But Medicare for All wasn’t among them. Rather, the most popular ideas—drawing more than 80% among both parties and independents—were banning surprise medical bills, capping drug prices and requiring insurers to cover the services that doctors prescribe. Only 23% of Republicans supported Medicare for All, a caution for any candidate who needs some measure of Republican support to win in November.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Kimberly Guilfoyle: President Trump said he is “looking at” firing his ambassador to Greece after revelations that she asked a donor to cover personal expenses in the lead-up to her confirmation hearing.

 

Katie Zacharia: Trump said the new White House press secretary would hold her first briefing at 9:30 a.m. ET.

 

Trump’s Tuesday: The president is scheduled to travel to Wasilla, Alaska, where he will hold a midterm rally at 6:30 p.m. ET. Later he is scheduled to leave Alaska and stay overnight in Las Vegas.

What I’m Following

 
 
JUSTIN SULLIVAN/GETTY IMAGES
 

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife. The Republican nominee in the hard-fought Texas Senate race was at a New Year’s Eve 2024 celebration in Dubai with the two accused men, among other revelers, according to a video of the gathering reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, details of which were contained in court filings and confirmed by people familiar with the matter. Trump endorsed Paxton over incumbent Texas Sen. John Cornyn this spring although he was told that damaging revelations were likely to surface about Paxton, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump was dismissive, saying there would be more negative material about Democratic nominee James Talarico.

 

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C., as part of a criminal investigation. The probe is immigration-related, said a person familiar with the matter. Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, has long been a top target for attacks from Trump and conservatives.

 

A judge scolded the Trump administration for cutting down golf course trees. The federal judge overseeing litigation challenging President Trump’s plan to overhaul a Washington, D.C., public golf course said the administration violated her instructions by cutting down hundreds of trees around East Potomac Golf Links on short notice over the weekend. On Monday, she temporarily barred further tree removal and said the government had lost credibility.
